articles.title: FBI seizes $1.2 billion in crypto stolen from Binance in record $6.3 billion heist
articles.summary: The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said Thursday that US authorities had seized or secured court authorisation to seize more than $1.2 billion
articles.body: The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said Thursday that US authorities had seized or secured court authorisation to seize more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency stolen last month from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. The recovery forms part of a wider effort by US authorities and private-sector companies to track down funds taken in what is regarded as the biggest cryptocurrency heist in history.The October theft involved approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets and has been attributed by the FBI to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group. The US government and private-sector partners have so far managed to freeze more than $2.7 billion of the stolen cryptocurrency. The Justice Department said it had obtained court authorisation to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of those assets, reported AP.The latest action is part of Washington's efforts to disrupt North Korea's alleged use of cybercrime to generate funds for its government and illicit weapons programme. US authorities have repeatedly accused Pyongyang of using sophisticated cyberattacks to steal digital assets and evade international sanctions.How did the $6.3 billion Binance heist happen?The incident took place on October 29, when hackers drained approximately $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance wallets used to process transactions. The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes, according to blockchain records analysed by cybersecurity firms.The precise method used to breach Binance's systems remains unclear. The exchange initially suspected that a laptop had been compromised but later said its investigation had uncovered additional points of breach.Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said the attackers had compromised Binance's transaction-signing infrastructure, which authorises transfers and allows funds to be moved out of wallets. In simple terms, the hackers may not have needed to steal the actual wallet keys but instead gained control over the system that authorised the release of funds.Binance had said its investigation was continuing, while its co-CEO Richard Teng assured users that losses would be covered through the company's Secure Asset Fund for Users and its own resources.How were the stolen funds tracked and frozen?After draining the wallets, the attackers attempted to move the cryptocurrency across different wallets and blockchains to avoid detection and prevent the funds from being frozen.A significant portion of the stolen assets was held in stablecoins such as Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC. Unlike decentralised cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, stablecoins can be frozen remotely by their issuers, making it possible for companies to block suspicious transactions when alerted by investigators.Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said the attackers attempted to convert hundreds of millions of dollars in stablecoins into Ethereum to move the assets beyond the reach of issuers. The firm tracked $325 million in stablecoin conversions into approximately $285 million worth of Ethereum over nearly 20 minutes.However, cryptocurrency companies, investigators and law enforcement agencies began freezing funds within hours of the attack. Chainalysis said the first freezes began at around 5:14 pm Eastern Time on October 29.The US government and private-sector partners have since frozen more than $2.7 billion worth of the stolen assets. The latest court authorisation covers more than $1.2 billion. Such cases generally involve forfeiture proceedings, in which the government files a claim before a judge determines who has a legitimate right to the recovered assets.The FBI has attributed the Binance theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-backed hacking group accused of targeting cryptocurrency exchanges, decentralised finance platforms and investors to generate funds for the regime.Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said its investigators strengthened the link after observing funds stolen from Binance being mixed with cryptocurrency taken in a separate attack on exchange Bitget, which had also been attributed to North Korean hackers.North Korea has repeatedly been accused by US authorities of carrying out cryptocurrency thefts to generate revenue for its government and circumvent international sanctions. The funds are alleged to help finance the country's weapons programmes, including its prohibited nuclear and ballistic missile activities.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Oil prices set for second weekly fall as Trump hardens stance on Iran, keeps military option open
articles.summary: Oil prices were largely steady on Friday but remained on track for a second consecutive weekly decline, extending a retreat from recent highs as
articles.body: Oil prices were largely steady on Friday but remained on track for a second consecutive weekly decline, extending a retreat from recent highs as expectations of a prolonged US blockade on Iran eased fears of an immediate escalation in the conflict. However, fresh threats from President Donald Trump and attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure continued to pose risks to Middle East supplies.Brent crude futures were little changed at $95.41 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) fell 20 cents, or 0.25 per cent, to $88.52 at 0242 GMT, reported Reuters.Brent was headed for a 2.4 per cent weekly decline, following a 16% plunge the previous week. WTI was set to fall 2.5 per cent, after losing 13 per cent last week.Oil prices had tumbled earlier this month after Trump played down the possibility of renewed strikes on Iran, with Brent settling at its lowest level since late August on November 9. Prices subsequently recovered over the next two sessions as attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and oil tankers heightened concerns over supply disruptions.The latest decline came after Trump said the United States did not need a deal with Iran to end the conflict, indicating that Washington would maintain its blockade on Iranian oil shipments, trade and economic activity.In a separate interview with Salem News Channel on Thursday, Trump issued a fresh warning to Tehran over alleged threats against American officials, saying those responsible for an attack on US officials "will not exist any longer".Read more: Trump warns Iran against targeting US officialsAsked whether he would hesitate to use military force to stop Iran from threatening US allies and ships, Trump replied: "No hesitation." He also said further military action was possible immediately if the situation warranted it.The remarks underline the uncertainty surrounding the conflict even as crude prices have retreated from recent highs. Trump also claimed that the US had complete control over the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for oil exports from major Middle Eastern producers.Shipping risks remain elevated. Iran's military said on Thursday that four oil tankers had been hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings. Reuters could not immediately verify the account.Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group also claimed to have attacked a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, an oil facility in Yanbu and an Aramco building in Riyadh.Adding to downward pressure on prices, US crude inventories rose by 4.7 million barrels to 414.4 million barrels in the week ended November 6, according to the Energy Information Administration. The increase was significantly higher than analysts' expectations of a 1.1-million-barrel draw in a Reuters poll.Despite the decline, the threat of further attacks on tankers and energy infrastructure means the outlook for oil prices remains closely tied to developments in the Middle East.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Tenant did not comply with 2005 Supreme Court eviction order and his son sold part of landlord’s property using parents’ settlement deed; buyer files suit against landlord but Madras HC strikes it off
articles.summary: In a tenant-landlord dispute, the former is asked to vacate the property by the Supreme Court.
articles.body: In a tenant-landlord dispute, the former is asked to vacate the property by the Supreme Court. But instead of complying, the tenant’s son ends up selling a share of the property and the buyer lodges a case against the landlord!As bizarre as it may sound, a recent Madras High Court throws light on how a tenant’s family continued to defy a Supreme Court eviction order and went on to sell the landlord’s property to two third-party purchasers.The buyers then asserted ownership rights on the strength of sale deeds executed by the tenant’s son. Read on to know what happenedWhat the case is aboutThe disputed property is situated in Vathikuppam and had been rented out. The Supreme Court, through its 2005 order directed the tenant to vacate the premises by August 31, 2006 and hand over peaceful possession to the landlord.The tenant, however, did not vacate the property. He and his wife had executed a registered settlement deed in favour of their son on August 10, 2001. Their son subsequently transferred the property through two registered sale deeds. One of the sale deeds was executed in January, 2012.One of the buyers alleged that the landlord’s family was interfering with her claimed peaceful possession of the property and approached the court seeking a permanent injunction.She was aggrieved by the developments and initiated legal proceedings against the landlord and his family. She sought a permanent injunction restraining them from interfering with her claimed peaceful possession and enjoyment of the property.When the landlord questioned how the tenant’s son could sell the property, the son relied on the settlement deed executed by his parents in his favour.After the landlord and his legal heirs learnt of these transactions, they approached the District Registrar, Puducherry, seeking cancellation of the settlement deed and the sale deeds.In a 2015 order, the registrar cancelled the sale deed executed in one of the buyer’s favour.The case went on to Madras High Court, which ruled in favour of the landlord’s family by striking off the buyer’s suit seeking permanent injunction.Why did the landlord’s family win while the buyer lost?The Madras High Court observed: “In the case in hand, it is a text book case where the tenant in the suit property, in spite of giving an undertaking before the Hon’ble Supreme Court to vacate and hand over the premises, managed to create a settlement deed in favour of his son, who, in turn, created two sale deeds.”The Madras High Court noted that the buyer had failed to disclose the earlier legal proceedings, including the Supreme Court’s eviction order, while seeking an injunction against the landlord’s family.It observed that the original tenant’s decision to execute a settlement deed in favour of his son, followed by the son transferring the property through two sale deeds to subsequent purchasers, amounted to contumacious conduct and was tantamount to contempt of court.The High Court also pointed out that the landlord and his family had been forced to run from pillar to post despite having prevailed in the earlier litigation, which had reached the Supreme Court in 2005.The court held that the buyer's suit amounted to a clear abuse of the judicial process and re-litigation.The High Court further observed that the matter warranted the exercise of its supervisory powers under Article 227 of the Constitution of India to prevent any further miscarriage of justice. It held that invoking this jurisdiction was necessary in the circumstances of the case.In 2014, the second buyer who acquired the property, moved the court through a writ petition challenging an order passed by the Tahsildar in connection with the disputed property. The Madras High Court rejected her petition on April 21, 2023, ruling that she had no rights over the landlord’s property and describing her occupation as illegal. It also ordered her eviction with police assistance.Kalpit Khandelwal, Partner at Aekom Legal, told ET that the buyer’s claim to the property hinged on the title held by the person who sold it to her, the tenant’s son. His claim, in turn, was based on a settlement deed executed by his parents, notwithstanding the Supreme Court’s direction requiring his father to vacate the premises.The Madras High Court found that the buyer had concealed details of the earlier legal proceedings.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Anthropic IPO six times oversubscribed as AI firm targets record $1.4 trillion valuation
articles.summary: Anthropic’s upcoming initial public offering (IPO) has attracted orders for about six times the number of shares available, signalling strong investor
articles.body: Anthropic’s upcoming initial public offering (IPO) has attracted orders for about six times the number of shares available, signalling strong investor appetite for what could become the biggest stock market listing in history.The strong demand for shares in the maker of the Claude artificial intelligence (AI) models could leave some prospective investors with smaller allocations than expected. Bankers have told investors that the company plans to prioritise existing backers, according to a Bloomberg News report citing people familiar with the matter.The reported level of demand and other details of the offering could still change.The company and some of its existing shareholders are seeking to raise as much as $64.4 billion through the IPO, while a separate private placement is expected to bring in another $26 billion. Together, the two transactions could raise around $90.4 billion, potentially making it the largest fundraising exercise of its kind.Anthropic is offering 825 million shares at a proposed price range of $70 to $78 apiece. Its shares are expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19 under the ticker symbol ANT. The company is targeting a fully diluted valuation of about $1.4 trillion.The IPO demand comes even as the AI industry faces questions over its dependence on advanced chips and the enormous spending required to develop and run AI models.Nvidia, a key strategic partner of Anthropic, has agreed to purchase about $10 billion worth of shares as part of the $26 billion private placement. Other technology companies participating in the placement include Google, Microsoft, AMD, Broadcom, Micron and TSMC, according to the company's filing.Anthropic has committed tens of billions of dollars towards securing access to advanced computing infrastructure, including chips needed to train and operate its AI models.Revenue growth supports valuationAnthropic’s rapid revenue growth is a key factor underpinning its ambitious valuation. The company reported a revenue run rate of $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from the end of September, according to its filing.The figure stood at $65 billion at the end of July, Bloomberg News had earlier reported. The company calculates its revenue run rate by annualising consumption-based fees over a 28-day period and subscription fees for a single month.Anthropic has also stepped up efforts to attract investors ahead of the listing. Its chief executive officer, Dario Amodei, is scheduled to take part in a live-streamed event with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon on Friday.Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the IPO, with 20 other banks participating in the offering.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: India plans its largest strategic oil reserve in Odisha at Rs 8,571 crore cost, adding 4 million tonnes of storage as Strait of Hormuz disruptions expose supply risks
articles.summary: India is stepping up efforts to enhance its strategic petroleum reserves, especially in wake of the Middle East crisis and the oil supply shock it has
articles.body: India is stepping up efforts to enhance its strategic petroleum reserves, especially in wake of the Middle East crisis and the oil supply shock it has brought about. The government is looking for private investors to develop the country’s largest strategic petroleum reserve in Odisha.India is stepping up efforts to strengthen its strategic crude storage following the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, which exposed the country’s vulnerability to sudden supply interruptions. The strait’s abrupt closure cut off around 40% of India’s crude supplies, leaving refiners scrambling to source alternative cargoes from across the world, often at higher costs.Indian Strategic Petroleum Reserves Ltd, the state-owned company responsible for operating the country’s strategic oil reserves, has issued separate tenders for developing the Odisha facility and leasing out part of the Visakhapatnam storage capacity.India’s largest strategic oil reserveThe project is estimated to cost Rs 8,571 crore. The proposed facility at Chandikhol will have the capacity to hold four million tonnes (MT) of crude oil, expanding the country’s existing strategic storage capacity by 80%.The government is offering financial support of up to Rs 5,142 crore for the project, according to an ET report. According to the tender documents, the contract will go to the bidder that seeks the lowest grant.Separately, the Centre plans to lease out nearly half of the storage capacity at its operational strategic petroleum reserve in Visakhapatnam. The arrangement will cover around 524,000 tonnes of capacity for three years, with an option to extend the lease by a further four years.Both moves come as oil producers in West Asia look for storage options outside the region to bypass the transit bottleneck created by the war in Iran and the prolonged disruption to energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.Last month, Saudi Arabia announced plans to start storing oil in Singapore’s rock caverns next year. The country already has crude storage facilities in Japan and South Korea. The UAE, which holds some of its crude in India’s strategic reserves, announced in June that it intended to store larger quantities in the country.The deadline for submitting bids for the new Odisha project is February 26, 2027, while bids for the Visakhapatnam storage lease must be submitted by December 1, 2026.The government has also asked Oil and Natural Gas Corp to develop 1.75 million tonnes of strategic storage capacity in Mangaluru. The state-owned oil producer approved the proposal in July.The proposed strategic reserve at Chandikhol has been under consideration since 2018, when the Cabinet cleared plans for two additional facilities: a four-million-tonne reserve in Odisha and a 2.5-million-tonne facility at Padur in Karnataka. Both projects were envisaged under the public-private partnership model to reduce the financial burden on the government.These facilities constituted the second phase of India’s strategic petroleum reserve (SPR) programme. The first phase involved building three storage facilities at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur, with a combined capacity of 5.03 million tonnes. Commissioned over the past decade, the three facilities were built at a total cost of Rs 4,098 crore.Last year, Megha Engineering & Infrastructures Ltd secured the contract to construct the 2.5-million-tonne facility at Padur as part of the second phase.The Chandikhol project, however, faced delays, partly because of the land acquisition process. According to the tender documents, the acquisition of around 400 acres at the site has now reached an advanced stage.The government also spent several years finalising a commercial structure that would attract private investors to the project. Under the model, it will provide a grant covering up to 60% of the project cost. The selected bidder will be responsible for developing and operating the commercial-cum-strategic petroleum reserve under the design, build, finance, operate and transfer model.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: 3 Indian-origin CEOs in race to replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia chief
articles.summary: Three Indian-origin technology executives, Sanjay Mehrotra, Nikesh Arora and Thomas Kurian, are among the names emerging in discussions over who could
articles.body: Three Indian-origin technology executives, Sanjay Mehrotra, Nikesh Arora and Thomas Kurian, are among the names emerging in discussions over who could succeed Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia after the chipmaker's co-founder stepped down with immediate effect on Thursday.Mehrotra, CEO of Micron Technology, Arora, who heads cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks, and Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, feature among the potential contenders as Nvidia begins looking for a permanent replacement for Huang, who led the company for more than three decades, as per multiple reports.Nvidia announced Huang's resignation amid mounting scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO, while the company said its board would consider both internal and external candidates. Longtime director Harvey Jones has also been appointed as Nvidia's first-ever board chairman.According to Bloomberg, Nvidia has engaged an outside firm to identify potential candidates for the position. The search is expected to be challenging, given Huang's central role in transforming the company from a graphics chipmaker into one of the world's most valuable technology firms and a dominant supplier of artificial intelligence processors.Mehrotra brings decades of semiconductor industry experience to the discussion. He has led Micron through the industry's boom-and-bust cycles, with the company's shares rising more than 2,700% during his tenure, driven in part by surging demand for memory chips linked to AI infrastructure.Arora has led Palo Alto Networks since 2018, overseeing its expansion in AI-powered cybersecurity. Before joining the company, he served as president and chief operating officer of SoftBank and spent a decade at Google.Kurian, meanwhile, heads Google Cloud, one of the major players in the global cloud computing and artificial intelligence market. His responsibilities span cloud infrastructure, enterprise software and AI services, giving him experience managing large-scale technology operations and relationships with major corporate customers.Other names in the succession discussion include Nvidia CFO Kress and vice-president Ian Buck, who helped develop CUDA, the software platform that made Nvidia's graphics processors central to modern AI computing. External possibilities include Arm CEO Rene Haas and Apple's chief hardware officer Johny Srouji.What we know about Huang's resignationNvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned with immediate effect following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence agencies of being a Chinese spy. The company has appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while considering internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, apologised to his wife, children and employees, admitting he had been “unfaithful to my wife”. The allegations have triggered national security concerns and calls for investigations in the US. Nvidia has maintained that there is no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? articles.title: OMCs continue to face petrol, diesel losses despite easing crude prices: Jefferies
articles.summary: Oil marketing companies (OMCs) continue to incur losses on the sale of petrol and diesel, although the extent of these losses has narrowed following a
articles.body: Oil marketing companies (OMCs) continue to incur losses on the sale of petrol and diesel, although the extent of these losses has narrowed following a decline in crude oil prices, according to a report by brokerage firm Jefferies.Marketing losses on petrol have fallen to Rs 12 per litre, while those on diesel have eased to Rs 27 per litre, based on 15-day average pricing, the report said.In October, the corresponding losses stood at Rs 22 per litre for petrol and Rs 28 per litre for diesel.Jefferies attributed the improvement to a decline in the Indian crude basket price, which has eased to $97 per barrel from $120 per barrel in October."With the Indian crude basket price easing to $97/ bbl ($120/bbl in Oct-26), the current losses on petrol/diesel have come down to Rs12/27 per liter (Rs22/28 in Oct-26)," the report said.Despite the reduction in losses, marketing margins on both fuels remain in negative territory, indicating continued pressure on OMCs' fuel marketing operations. Jefferies noted that petrol and diesel margins had remained largely negative through much of 2026, with losses widening during periods of higher crude prices.Crude supply improves, but freight rates remain highThe report also highlighted an improvement in global crude supply conditions. Crude oil exports from the Middle East have returned to pre-war levels, while Saudi Arabia's crude production rose in October to its highest level in four years.Physical premiums have also fallen to zero. However, freight rates remain very elevated, while diesel spreads continue to stay above $80, adding to pressure in the oil market.On the gas front, spot liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices averaged $31 per million British thermal units (mmbtu), down 2% week-on-week. Jefferies noted that domestic affordability remained stretched at current price levels.European Union gas storage stood at 72%, compared with 82% during the same period last year. With colder weather reducing storage levels, the brokerage expects gas prices to remain elevated as the winter season approaches.Petrochemical margins improveThe report also pointed to an improvement in petrochemical margins over the past fortnight.A sharp decline in naphtha prices, alongside firm prices of polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP), has widened spreads in the petrochemical segment.Overall, while lower crude prices have reduced the losses OMCs incur on petrol and diesel sales, their fuel marketing margins remain negative. Elevated freight rates and diesel spreads continue to weigh on the broader oil market, according to Jefferies.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? articles.title: Russia's diesel exports surge 100% after Trump lifts sanctions; not a single shipment reaches US
articles.summary: Russia nearly doubled its diesel exports in October after US President Donald Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase
articles.body: Russia nearly doubled its diesel exports in October after US President Donald Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase fuel supplies to global markets. However, none of the additional shipments has reached the US so far, with tankers originally headed for American buyers changing course amid opposition to the move and concerns over sanctions.Russia exported around 271,000 barrels of diesel per day in October, compared with 135,000 barrels per day in September, according to data provider Kpler. Instead of reaching the US, the additional Russian fuel went to markets such as Brazil and Turkey, allowing Moscow to increase sales despite uncertainty over the proposed American shipments, according to a report by The Financial Times.At least two tankers initially headed for the US have changed course in recent weeks. Another vessel carrying Russian diesel, the Agioi Fanendes, remains off the US East Coast awaiting a buyer. The White House said negotiations with the vessel's owner were continuing.The increase in exports came after Washington pressed Ukraine to pause attacks on Russian oil refineries and Trump announced an agreement with Putin on October 9.What was the Trump-Putin diesel deal?Trump announced the deal last month following a conversation with Putin, saying Russia had agreed to supply additional diesel to the US and global markets to bring down fuel prices.In a social media post, Trump had said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes after that. He also said Russia would deliver another three million tonnes within a short period.The announcement came as diesel prices in the US were rising sharply, putting pressure on consumers and businesses that depend on the fuel for transport, agriculture and other operations. High fuel prices were also a political concern for Trump's Republican Party ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections.To facilitate the proposed supplies, the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued General License No. 135 on October 9. The licence temporarily authorised transactions involving the sale, delivery and import of Russian diesel that would otherwise have been restricted under US sanctions. It was issued for six months, allowing such transactions through April 2027.A White House official told the Financial Times that additional Russian diesel entering global markets would help ease prices for American consumers, even if the fuel was not delivered directly to the US.“As the President has said, this is a deal for the world. This deal was made to add diesel supply to the global market — lowering prices for Americans and the world — which is exactly what will be done,” the official said, as quoted by FT.Why deal sparked controversy?The diesel agreement came after efforts in the US Congress to increase economic pressure on Russia over its war in Ukraine. One major measure was the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, signed into law by Trump on September 18.The legislation provided for additional sanctions against Russia and tariffs on Russian goods, as well as duties on imports from major buyers of Russian oil and gas and countries facilitating sanctions evasion. However, on October 16, Trump issued an executive order waiving the application of these measures, citing national interests and the need to pursue a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine. It allowed up to 100% tariffs on countries buying Russian oil.A separate legal challenge has been raised by New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill over the proposed diesel imports. In a letter dated November 2, she argued that the Treasury Department's October 9 licence conflicts with the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, passed by Congress in April 2022. That law prohibits imports of Russian energy products, including diesel.Sherrill argued that the 2022 law does not give the president or the Treasury Department blanket authority to waive the import prohibition through a licence. She also said the administration had not met the conditions required to lift the ban and warned port and terminal operators that accepting Russian diesel could expose them to civil and criminal penalties. “New Jersey will not stand by while Donald Trump supports Vladimir Putin at the expense of Americans,” she said.Will Russia continue increasing diesel exports?The recent rise in exports may not last. Ukraine resumed attacks on Russian refineries on October 30, following a two-week pause. Russia has also extended its diesel export ban until the end of January, although some exceptions will be allowed.Richard Bronze, head of geopolitics at consultancy Energy Aspects, said the increase in exports reflected Russian refineries' ability to raise production during the pause in Ukrainian attacks. “If we want to attribute it, it would be the US pressure and Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire,” he said.However, Bronze expects Russian diesel exports to be “very lacklustre” in the coming months, as quoted by FT. “Russian refinery operations remain under significant pressure. We expect them to remain constrained around 4mn b/d in the near term, with limited prospects for a meaningful recovery as attacks continue,” said Sumit Ritolia, an analyst at Kpler.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Taxpayer filed Form 10-IEA for old regime but chose new regime in ITR, triggering Rs 1.41 lakh demand; ITAT rejects his plea for new regime but asks taxman to allow eligible deductions under old regime
articles.summary: You opt out of the new income tax regime by filing Form 10-IEA, but while filing your income tax return opt for the new regime.
articles.body: You opt out of the new income tax regime by filing Form 10-IEA, but while filing your income tax return opt for the new regime. Under what regime will your return be processed - new or old?In one such case a taxpayer ended up making contrary choices and the Income Tax Department processed his return under the old tax regime and raised a tax demand. He fought the tax addition believing that his choice in ITR should override Form 10-IEA.The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), Mumbai, rejected the taxpayer's argument that the selection in his return should prevail. However, it gave him partial relief. Read to know what happened.What the case is aboutThe case concerns a man’s income tax return for assessment year 2025-26. The taxpayer had opted for the new income tax regime in the preceding assessment year, 2024-25. On August 31, 2025, when he filed Form 10-IEA he opted out of the new regime and was taxed under the old income regime.However, when he filed his income tax return on September 16, 2025, declaring a total income of Rs 33,88,170, he selected the option indicating that he did not wish to opt out of the new tax regime. This was contrary to the choice that was recorded in the form he had filed earlier.The CPC processed his return under Section 143(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, on January 29, 2026. It took Form 10-IEA into account and raised a demand of Rs 1,41,480. Joshi sought rectification, but the CPC rejected his request under Section 154 on February 17, 2026.He then appealed to the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), who upheld the adjustment. The appellate authority reasoned that the taxpayer had opted out of the new tax regime through the prescribed form, making the contrary selection in his return an incorrect claim.Before the Mumbai ITAT, the taxpayer argued that the CPC should have followed the option selected in his return instead of relying on Form 10-IEA. His counsel cited a Pune ITAT ruling in Akshay Nitin Malu v. Income Tax Officer, arguing that the choice declared in the return should be respected.He also challenged the processing of his return on the ground that the CPC had not issued prior intimation of the proposed adjustment. For this, he relied on a Bombay High Court ruling in Rallis India Ltd v. Central Processing Centre.As an alternative, the man argued that if the old tax regime applied because of Form 10-IEA, he should be allowed the deductions available under that regime. His claims included Rs 1.5 lakh under Section 80C, Rs 50,000 under Section 80D and Rs 50,000 under Section 80TTB.What ITAT Mumbai saidThe tribunal examined whether the taxpayer could rely on the selection in his return when it contradicted the prescribed form he had already filed.The bench noted that the taxpayer had opted for the new income regime in assessment year 2024-25 and subsequently filed Form 10-IEA to move to the old income tax regime for assessment year 2025-26.Under Section 115BAC, taxpayers with business or professional income must exercise the relevant option in the prescribed manner, and the rules restrict when that choice can be withdrawn.The tribunal held that the selection in the return could not override the prescribed form.It observed: “In our opinion, once a specific form has been prescribed for opting out of the new tax regime, the assessee cannot be permitted to choose for the new tax regime otherwise than filing said form under the provisions of the Act.”It also distinguished the Pune ITAT ruling cited by the taxpayer. In that case, the taxpayer had filed Form 10-IE to opt out of the new regime and had also filed the return under the old regime.This case was different because the form and the return indicated conflicting choices. The tribunal noted: “But in the instant case, facts are different. In the Form 10-IE filed, assessee is opting out of new tax regime and choosing old tax regime. But in the return of income, wrong box has been ticked.”The bench also rejected the taxpayer’s argument that the CPC had processed his return without prior intimation. It had asked him to produce evidence from the income tax portal showing that no intimation had been sent by email or physical letter, but he did not provide the requested material.The tribunal distinguished the Rallis India case because the department had acknowledged there that no notice or proposed adjustment had been issued. It therefore dismissed this ground of appeal.The taxpayer, however, succeeded on his alternative plea concerning deductions. The tribunal held that if the old income tax regime applied on the basis of Form 10-IEA, the deductions available under that regime also had to be considered.It observed: “If CPC is holding that assessee has opted out of the new tax regime and old tax regime of this is applicable, then the deduction entitled under the old tax regime should be allowed to the assessee.”The bench set aside the appellate order on this limited issue and restored the matter to the Assessing Officer to examine the eligible deductions. The tribunal also recorded that “In our opinion, there is a merit in the submission of the assessee.”The ITAT pronounced its order on September 17, 2026, and partly allowed the appeal. It did not cancel the Rs 1,41,480 demand outright or automatically grant all the deductions claimed. The Assessing Officer must examine the taxpayer's eligibility for deductions under the old regime.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? Join the TOI Money Masterclass.

articles.title: The AI boom was built around Jensen Huang. Now what?
articles.summary: Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia in scandal leaves the company without its visionary leader. It also leaves a major void for the AI industry, where Huang was kingmaker in inking deals to support the tech boom.
articles.body: Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia in scandal leaves the company without its visionary leader. It also leaves a major void for the AI industry, where Huang was kingmaker in inking deals to support the tech boom. Under Huang’s leadership, Nvidia became more than a chipmaker: It guaranteed deals for data centers, invested heavily in AI startups and even backed the companies that bought its products. Huang put Nvidia at the core of AI financing, and the CEO himself championed some of the industry’s biggest deals. His departure puts a spotlight on whether the ecosystem he crafted could fracture — and whether that would spell trouble for the AI boom that has helped prop up the US stock market and become a driving force of economic growth. “It’s hard to overstate his personal role in all of this,” said Neil Wilson, a strategist at investment bank Saxo. “Huang was key in Nvidia being the backer of last resort across the AI ecosystem, really underpinning a lot of the financing and infrastructure guarantees,” he said. Nvidia backstopped deals, like committing $105 billion in August for an OpenAI data center. The company has a major equity stake in the neocloud CoreWeave, emerging as an important financial backer and confidence booster. Nvidia is expected to take a $10 billion stake in Anthropic’s initial public offering. Nvidia makes the graphics processing units that power AI models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. But the company has also been “the central bank of AI,” Jay Goldberg, senior analyst at Seaport Research Partners, told CNN. The company also functions like a venture capitalist, Goldberg noted, investing in companies to fuel their growth and help them get ahead in an industry that requires massive amounts of capital. “Circular financing” has emerged as a term to describe Nvidia’s financial agreements, because the company is backing the companies that, in turn, buy its products. Goldberg said a more accurate term would be “very aggressive vendor financing.” The company’s financial commitments in the AI boom have grown to the point that it had to address the associated risks in its latest quarterly earnings filing. “Commitments, guarantees and other commercial arrangements expose us to financial, counterparty and execution risks and may not provide anticipated benefits,” Nvidia said in its most recent quarterly earnings report. Huang’s sudden fall from grace puts that financing strategy in question. He resigned amid revelations extramarital affairs and a board investigation into whether he was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.” Just three months ago, after committing the $105 billion for the OpenAI data center, Huang brought together six major financial institutions — Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR — to agree to treat Nvidia’s AI infrastructure as an asset class to write debt against, with aims of mobilizing over $500 billion for the AI boom. “That was all driven by [Huang],” Goldberg said, adding that the deal isn’t finalized, and he expects it will come under additional review (and could even fall through). Nvidia and the neoclouds Nvidia’s central role in AI financing is directly related to the so-called neoclouds, or companies that rent out compute to power the boom. Nvidia, as the primary provider of technology to power AI, has reaped massive profits in recent years. The company has used its cash to invest in neoclouds like CoreWeave and also provide backstops by guaranteeing to step in and provide revenue if they can’t sell all the compute capacity from Nvidia’s GPUs. If Nvidia loses its savvy as an AI financier, it muddies the outlook for the neocloud industry, which relies on Nvidia as a bedrock to help issue those guarantees that help companies lock in more affordable interest rates. In October, when CoreWeave’s bond yields spiked, the situation only calmed after Huang stepped in and expressed confidence in the company’s future. “I’m optimistic,” Huang told Bloomberg News on October 15. CoreWeave stock rallied 6% that day, snapping a three-day slide. “This just raises the pressure on some of the smaller neoclouds’ ability to raise capital,” Goldberg said. “When we lose Jensen, we lose a lot of the animating force that’s been driving the industry,” Goldberg said. “So, the world just feels a little bit smaller without him.” Nvidia at the center — for now Huang’s financing strategy not only supports the growth of the AI boom, but effectively secured Nvidia’s status as the axis on which everything was connected. The AI industry’s existing long-term agreements mean the near-term outlook likely stays the same, Goldberg said. But, over time, Nvidia’s ability to deploy the same creative financing strategies could become less certain and potentially slow the industry’s expansion. While Nvidia announced Thursday that Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, would be interim CEO, potentially reassuring investors, replacing Huang’s dealmaking expertise will be a much bigger challenge. “He was not only the chief technology architect … but he was also the capital allocator,” Ted Mortonson, tech strategist at Baird, told CNN. “With him leaving, it leaves a huge void,” Mortonson said. Nvidia also faces competition for its role as the core provider of compute, with other semiconductor companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom already building alternatives to the company’s GPUs. Uncertainty over Nvidia’s role could put pressure on other tech companies, or the hyperscalers like Alphabet and Amazon, to step up as the capital allocator Nvidia has been. But it remains to be seen who can champion the industry and execute dealmaking like Huang. Huang’s dual role as the man who understood the tech and the dealmaker who understood the financing was a unique combination that contributed to his star-status role, Mortonson said. Huang gave Nvidia the clout and ability to dictate terms on pricing and deals, analysts said. Without Huang, that ability becomes less apparent. “Jensen’s successor will not have the same latitude or deference to pursue circular deals and pursue aggressive sales tactics,” Mike O’Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading, told CNN in an email. “There’s the quantifiable and the unquantifiable,” said Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, a fund focused on founder-led companies. “There are things you can’t put in a spreadsheet, right?,” Monaghan said. “He has that aura, plus all of that engineering knowledge, plus all of the 33 years of building all this stuff. You just can’t replace that.” “Jensen knew where to put his own capital to help grow the ecosystem, and that walks out the door with him,” Monaghan said. Demand for AI is robust. Anthropic’s revenue in the third quarter soared more than 1,000% year-over-year, a sign that people are adopting and paying for AI. Companies are likely to keep investing in infrastructure to meet the demand. But investors ultimately want to see those investment turn into profits, or may begin to question whether the massive spending is justified. Huang’s departure shakes the foundation of the sprawling web of financing that has come to define the AI economy. A slowdown in dealmaking could exacerbate cost pressures, spell trouble for smaller companies and create added headwinds that could hamper the AI trade. “The risk is less about chip demand than about the money,” David Rosenberg, president and founder at Rosenberg Research, wrote in a note. “Nvidia’s stakes, guarantees and backstops are what tie the AI trade together, so the weakest links are the borrowers who depend on Nvidia’s support.”

articles.title: Trump’s tariffs face a new threat: Republicans
articles.summary: In the two years since President Donald Trump unveiled a slew of aggressive tariffs on America’s global trading partners, the prospect of stock market backlash has been the biggest restraint on his agenda. The midterms may have just changed that.
articles.body: In the two years since President Donald Trump unveiled a slew of aggressive tariffs on America’s global trading partners, the prospect of stock market backlash has been the biggest restraint on his agenda. The midterms may have just changed that. Despite a steady drumbeat of polls showing Americans’ disdain for Trump’s tariffs, Republican lawmakers largely avoided publicly challenging the president’s trade agenda, seeing the political fallout from standing in his way as too great. But last week’s election results suggest there may also be a steep political price for that loyalty. Democrats notched significant victories at the polls, flipping seats in historically Republican states where voters have been hit hard by Trump’s tariffs, from agriculture-heavy states like Iowa and Kansas to northern border states such as Maine and Michigan. “Many Republicans were kind of whistling by the political graveyard by ignoring the tariff issue, but now it’s come front and center,” Brian Darling, a Republican strategist and former counsel to Republican Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, said. “Republicans are going to have to take a hard look in the mirror and take a second look at their position on tariffs.” Opposition to tariffs has traditionally been a cornerstone of Republican economic policy, while Democrats have more often backed tariffs as a way to protect domestic industries and workers, particularly unionized ones. That made Trump’s sweeping use of tariffs, a cornerstone of his overarching agenda, a particularly uncomfortable departure for some Republicans, particularly those up for re-election who feared defeat in primaries if they crossed Trump. While one of Trump’s stated goals in imposing higher tariffs was to boost US-based employment, many employers have been reluctant to take on more workers, given the uncertain trade environment with Trump often altering policies. The impact on prices, by contrast, has been more direct. Tariffs have pushed up the cost of not only imported goods but also products made in the United States. About 26% of tariff increases are ultimately passed on to consumers, according to a September study by New York Federal Reserve economists. Nationally, two-thirds of voters said Trump’s tariffs hurt the national economy, according to nationwide results of CNN’s Voter Poll. Nearly the same share said they hurt the local economy, too. “Any member who is up for re-election in 2028 has got to be looking at what happened here in 2026 and wondering if they need to be more active opposing the tariffs so that this doesn’t become an attack line against them in 2028,” said Brian Pomper, co-leader of lobbying at the law firm Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld. Whether any newfound opposition can translate into meaningful change, however, is another question. ‘Mr. Veto’ Even if Republicans are willing to risk Trump’s ire, they face another major obstacle: his veto power. Congress could repeal the tariffs or restrict the president’s tariff authority with a simple majority in both chambers. But if the president vetoed the measure, lawmakers would need two-thirds majorities in the House and Senate to override him. With one Senate race and 12 House races still uncalled as of Thursday afternoon, Democrats and their independent allies hold 55 of the Senate’s 100 seats and 255 of the House’s 435 seats. Even if they voted unanimously, they would still need at least 12 Republicans in the Senate and 35 in the House to override a presidential veto. Without that level of Republican support, Trump could veto legislation seeking to rein in his tariff authority, a prospect he has made clear he is prepared to embrace. “I’ll become Mr. Veto,” Trump said in an Election Day interview on the New York Post’s Pod Force One before results came in. Still, even without enough votes to override a veto, growing Republican support for rolling back certain tariffs could give Trump an incentive to retreat on his own to avoid a fight with his party, Darling said. The White House, meanwhile, has signaled it has no plans to put the brakes on Trump’s tariff agenda. “Putting a stop to American workers, farmers, and businesses being ripped off by lopsided trade agreements has been a key foundation of President Trump’s Make America Great Again movement since he first came down the escalator. President Trump will never waver from putting Americans and America First,” White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNN in a statement. Still, Trump has shown some willingness to rein in certain tariffs. After markets plunged following his April 2 “Liberation Day” tariff announcement, he delayed many of the sweeping duties just a week later. He also showed signs of restraint ahead of the midterms: Less than two weeks before Election Day, he exempted products, including plywood and packaging materials, from the 50% duties on Canadian goods he imposed over the summer. That followed exemptions for road salt and cement. In both instances, now-defeated Republican Sen. Susan Collins took credit for securing the relief. Over the summer, Trump also threatened to double tariffs on Canadian cars to 50% starting January 1. A White House official told CNN that the administration is actively negotiating with Canada to finalize new trade terms, which could include revising the auto duties. Democrats see opening Democrats, meanwhile, have made clear that rolling back Trump’s tariffs will be a top priority when the new Congress convenes at the start of 2027, with Canadian tariffs emerging as an early target. House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next Speaker of the House, said immediately after the elections that repealing Trump’s tariffs should be among the party’s top priorities in its first 100 days. But Democrats may not be entirely unified in that effort, particularly when it comes to tariffs that enjoy support from organized labor. “There are still going to be some Democrats that are still kind of old-school labor union Dems that don’t go along with this,” said Scott Lincicome, vice president of general economics and trade at the Libertarian-leaning Cato Institute. Steel and aluminum tariffs, which Trump raised to 50%, could prove especially difficult to roll back given the strong backing they have among unions, he added. The Canadian tariffs could offer the clearest starting point for building bipartisan support. Trump imposed them under a Great Depression-era law that allows a president to set tariffs up to 50% when another country discriminates against American goods. No other president has applied it that way, though, and it is currently facing legal challenges. Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, who is expected to take over as chairman of the Senate Finance Committee in January, is leading the push in the Senate and has made the Canadian tariffs a focus. “Voters gave Democrats a mandate to rein in Trump’s tariffs that are raising prices all across our country, and to stop the president from abusing our trade laws in the future,” Wyden told CNN in a statement. “It is my hope that Republicans will acknowledge the election results and join Democrats to roll back Trump’s tariffs and lower prices for American families. If not, it will be crystal clear whose side Republicans are on,” he said. Republicans confront political cost Some Republicans have already begun acknowledging that the party’s approach to tariffs may have come at a political cost. Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz, whose state saw major Democratic gains in last week’s elections, pointed to voters’ frustration with the cost of living as a key factor behind the results. “Tariffs have made everything too expensive,” Cruz wrote in a post on X last week. “Understandably, people were pissed off, and elected Republicans didn’t do enough to address their very real pain,” he later added. But Cruz has repeatedly backed Trump’s tariff agenda in Congress. He voted against all five Senate resolutions in 2025 seeking to repeal the president’s tariffs, including measures targeting duties on Canada, Brazil and dozens of other countries. Republican Rep. Don Bacon, who is retiring, has been more willing to break with the president. He was among six Republicans who joined Democrats in February to vote to repeal Trump’s tariffs on Canada, in a rare rebuke of the president’s trade agenda. At the time, House Speaker Mike Johnson said Trump was “not upset” with Republicans who voted against the tariffs. “He understands what’s going on. It’s not going to affect or change his policy. He can veto these things if they come to it,” Johnson told CNN. Trump, however, subsequently took to Truth Social to issue a warning to Republicans considering similar defections. Bacon told CNN he wasn’t sure whether Republicans’ appetite for pushing back against Trump’s trade agenda had grown since the midterms. “It should,” he said. “Trump’s tariffs killed the GOP this election.”

articles.title: 'Will be resolved very soon': India on Scotch imports from UK amid bulk shipments held at ports
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The government is hopeful of resolving the dispute over bulk Scotch whisky shipments held at Indian ports within the next few days, commerce
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The government is hopeful of resolving the dispute over bulk Scotch whisky shipments held at Indian ports within the next few days, commerce secretary Rajesh Agrawal said on Friday.Agrawal said product classification was among the key concerns being discussed and that the Department of Revenue was working to address the issue."Department of Revenue is working to resolve it. Classification is among the key issues. It should be resolved very soon...We are very hopeful that it would be resolved in some days," Agrawal said, ANI reported.His remarks came after officials from the commerce and finance ministries met to discuss concerns raised by liquor companies over the classification of imported Scotch whisky.Representatives of the International Spirits and Wine Association of India (ISWAI) and the Confederation of Indian Alcoholic Beverage Companies (CIABC) also met Agrawal to flag the differences over customs duties.The dispute centres on whether bulk Scotch whisky imports qualify for the reduced 75% duty under the India-UK trade agreement, which came into effect in July, or should attract the 150% duty applicable to certain alcoholic preparations.Customs investigators argue that the 75% tariff concession under the trade pact applies only to finished products, such as bottled Scotch whisky, and not to bulk concentrates that undergo further processing.The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) has classified the imported goods as "compound alcoholic preparations", rather than finished whisky. This has led to a disagreement over the applicable Harmonised System (HS) code and the duty payable.Earlier a confidential November 4 memo from the DRI, reviewed by Reuters, directed customs commissioners across the country to continue applying the higher duty.It said importers were "incorrectly" claiming benefits under the India-UK trade pact for bulk Scotch shipments. The memo warned that any misclassification had "large-scale, recurring substantial revenue implications"."Preliminary investigation revealed that the imported goods are not finished whisky/brand/rum as such, but are concentrated/compound preparations which are subjected to further manufacturing," the memo said.The dispute has led to shipments belonging to several liquor companies being held at Indian ports.Companies affected include Pernod Ricard India, Diageo, Radico Khaitan and Allied Blenders and Distillers, according to people familiar with the matter.Pernod Ricard and Diageo each have more than 40 containers held at ports, while Bacardi has another five containers on hold, industry sources told Reuters.The delays could disrupt supplies, the sources said. Tax officials have also searched the offices of several companies, including Pernod Ricard and Diageo, and questioned executives in recent weeks.Around 80% of Scotch whisky imports from Britain by volume arrive in bulk and are subsequently used to manufacture Indian-Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL), which blends smaller quantities of Scotch with other spirits and ingredients.Scotch whisky exports to India were worth $335 million in 2024. The Scotch Whisky Association has estimated that the India-UK trade agreement could increase the value of this trade by $1.34 billion over five years.The International Spirits and Wines Association of India has cautioned that the dispute "risks undermining, in practice, an important market-access benefit negotiated and agreed between India and the United Kingdom".Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: The Nvidia scandal has hidden upside potential for the AI trade
articles.summary: Jensen Huang is out. The former CEO of Nvidia resigned after a rapid succession of damning news reports revealed multiple affairs.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang is out. The former CEO of Nvidia resigned after a rapid succession of damning news reports revealed multiple affairs, including one with a woman that US intelligence says is a Chinese spy and others with employees. The scandal is unequivocally damaging for Huang. And, at least in the short term, destabilizing for Nvidia, and detrimental to the AI trade .

The debacle highlights Nvidia's unbelievably high level of unmitigated key-person risk, which has caused an unmitigated disaster. Nvidia's leadership structure had little precedent, with 60 employees reporting directly to Huang. He never created a succession plan. And the company failed to develop a bench of public-facing managers that could quickly step into the top role.

The key-person risk extended to the entire AI trade. Huang was everywhere, seemingly, stumping for US tech dominance and an architect for an ecosystem of AI capital and hardware. If Nvidia was the "central bank of AI," Huang was the chair.

As chief economic adviser at Allianz, Mohamed El-Erian, wrote on X the night before Huang resigned, "This is no ordinary CEO. This is no ordinary company. This is no ordinary sector. This is no ordinary time." El-Erian said it's hard to see the fallout being contained to just one company.

But if Nvidia and the broader AI trade successfully weather the storm , it could amount to a huge win for both the company and sector.

Going forward, investors and analysts will judge Nvidia without the rose-colored glasses that Edison-like founders often invite. And in a world without Huang, the cult of visionary founder disintegrates. Only the numbers and arguments matter. If they're still good and compelling, the AI trade only looks more rock solid. Winning without your star player makes your team look good.

A useful analog here is Apple, with Steve Jobs' departure, rehire, and eventual succession to Tim Cook. After Jobs' first stint, the iPhone maker lost its way before Jobs came back to right the ship, eventually passing the torch to Tim Cook. Who, solid as he was, was certainly no Steve Jobs. (President Trump suggested that Nvidia pull Apple's Cook out of retirement.)

Huang might be an AI visionary who singlehandedly fostered the AI transformation. But in his wake, Nvidia and the AI trade may prove he wasn't so indispensable , just like Jobs was in the Cook era as Apple moved on.

(The Jobs comparison also brings up the question of whether Huang might return one day.)

Looking past a "dark day" for Nvidia and the US tech industry, Yorkville Ives' Dan Ives said "the US tech industry is still way ahead of China in the AI Revolution and this situation will sharpen the sword in the battle and arms race between the two countries."

articles.title: How Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia is threatening AI-powered economy
articles.summary: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia threatens the stability of the AI industry and the market as a whole, as experts express differing outlooks on the chipmaker’s future. Huang resigned as CEO of the company he built from the ground up, Nvidia’s board of directors announced Thursday, after The New York Times reported on a pair…
articles.body:
Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia threatens the stability of the AI industry and the market as a whole, as experts express differing outlooks on the chipmaker’s future.

Huang resigned as CEO of the company he built from the ground up, Nvidia’s board of directors announced Thursday , after The New York Times reported on a pair of extramarital affairs he had — one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Shares of Nvidia dipped on Thursday after Huang’s resignation, falling to less than $150 for the first time since June 2025.

While the company’s stock has since rebounded, the effects of Huang leaving Nvidia have yet to ripple through the economy.

“I don’t think today’s trading is really indicative of anything,” Dan Alpert, the executive chair at Westwood Capital, told The Hill.

“Everybody knew that the stock was going to tank this morning, and you know there’s a huge bunch of true believers in the AI space, and they thought they were getting a bargain,” Alpert added.

Huang’s departure from Nvidia, 33 years after he founded the company from a Denny’s, marked the end of an era. The Taiwanese American entrepreneur became an omnipresent and influential figure, as his company’s chips powered a technological revolution that is turning the world on its head.

Tech analyst Dan Ives highlighted the shocking nature of Huang’s exit, writing “What seemed impossible a week ago is now a reality” on Thursday morning.

“The old Jensen, the black leather jacket, the Godfather of AI, the rock star viewed as the face of the AI boom, is over and in the past,” wrote Ives , a partner at Yorkville Ives & Co.

Nvidia’s market power was evident in its reach across the tech industry. The chipmaker supplied graphics processing units (GPU) to the likes of Amazon, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI and Oracle.

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill understand the scale of Nvidia’s impact. Sen. Jim Justice (R-W.Va.) noted the “amazing” technology at the company’s disposal, saying the upheaval at the tech giant “will surely” have an effect on the economy.

“The magnitude of the impact, I can’t tell you,” Justice told The Hill. “But it could have a major impact.”

If the impact extends to the rest of the market, everyday Americans could face negative consequences. The Dow Jones Industrial Average , Nasdaq composite and S&P 500 all dipped by less than 0.4 percent on Thursday.

Nvidia, which has 19,000 employees across the country, paid $10 billion in federal and state income taxes in fiscal 2025, the company reported . The firm also works with government agencies, state and local authorities and universities, as AI reshapes the economy.

Ryuta Makino, a software and semiconductor research analyst at Gabelli Funds, predicted Nvidia “will continue to perform as usual” in the near term, noting the company’s deals for 2027 and 2028 are “locked up.”

But Makino said the industry may experience broader impacts in 2029 and 2030, saying Huang’s departure could “lower AI infrastructure spend in the long term,” as Nvidia will “likely” lose market share.

“This can also mean that lower efficiency gains on these servers equals lower AI efficiency and therefore the entire ecosystem will be worse overall,” Makino added.

Alpert raised another problem for Nvidia, one that implicates the entire AI industry. The company’s penchant for “circular” financing, whereby it invests in companies that purchase its chips, poses a “concern” for the economy, he said.

“The correlation between the circular finance arrangements with regard to both the data centers and the chips is massive, and … with these models becoming more efficient and more capable … nobody knows how much ‘compute’ is going to be required,” said Alpert, who equated circular financing to “Ponzi finance.”

Alpert added, “Anytime you have the buyer financed by the seller, you end up with misplaced price signals. You end up with … the seller taking credit risk to the buyer, and eventually the situation just eats itself.”

Ives, on the other hand, remains bullish on the future for Nvidia — now led by interim CEO Colette Kress, the company’s executive vice president and chief financial officer since 2013.

The tech giant “remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI Revolution,” Ives wrote, adding Nvidia is “roughly 2-3 years ahead” of the nearest competitor.

“The fundamentals have not changed overnight,” wrote Hendi Susanto, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds. “Demand for AI compute is still strong and customers will not cancel their orders; the roadmap for the next two years is in place.”

It is unclear whether Kress will become Nvidia’s permanent CEO. The company’s board, which also appointed Harvey Jones as its chair on Thursday, noted it will consider internal and external candidates for the CEO position.

President Trump, meanwhile, threw Apple executive chair Tim Cook’s name into the hat . Cook, who stepped down as Apple CEO over the summer, is the “only” person who can succeed Huang, Trump wrote Thursday on Truth Social .

For now, Kress will take over, with Nvidia set to report third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. Mark Malek, the chief investment officer at Siebert Financial, called Tuesday’s earnings call the “most important” in the company’s history.

“I will be listening less for the quarter and more for the backlog,” Malek wrote in a note. “Are the orders still the orders?”

The fallout from Huang’s reported affairs could create multiple problems for Kress, Nvidia and the AI industry, experts say.

One potential problem concerns the company’s ability to export chips to China, which lawmakers are calling to curb in the wake of the Times reporting on the former Nvidia CEO’s affair with Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy.

Trump greenlighted sales of Nvidia’s H20 and H200 chips to China last year , after Jensen Huang lobbied for fewer restrictions.

But lawmakers from both parties have called for harsher export controls in the wake of the scandal, arguing Nvidia sending its chips to Beijing threatens U.S. national security .

Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) argued Thursday there is “no reason” for the company to sell advanced AI chips to China.

Lieu asked, “Name one reason why we would do that?” before accusing Trump of allowing Nvidia to sell chips to China after Huang donated to the White House ballroom project .

Justice had a different view, saying a broad export ban is “too much of a scattergun approach” for Congress to take.

But Ives, consistently an optimist regarding AI and tech, remains an optimist. Although he lowered his stock valuation of Nvidia from $300 per share with Huang as CEO to $225 per share without him, the tech analyst said he is “not throwing in the white towel” for the company.

Thursday was “a dark day for Nvidia and the US tech industry and a black eye moment for Jensen and the legacy he built,” Ives wrote.

“HOWEVER … that said the US tech industry is still way ahead of China in the AI Revolution and this situation will sharpen the sword in the battle and arms race between the two countries,” Ives predicted.

Miranda Nazzaro and Julia Shapero contributed reporting.

articles.title: 'Dark pattern': Ola fined Rs 10 lakh for misleading pre-ride tip feature
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) on Friday imposed a fine of Rs 10 lakh on ride-hailing platform Ola over its \"pre-ride tip\"
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) on Friday imposed a fine of Rs 10 lakh on ride-hailing platform Ola over its "pre-ride tip" feature, terming the practice misleading.The authority directed ANI Technologies Private Limited, which operates Ola, to immediately stop seeking additional payments before confirming rides, calling the practice an unfair trade practice and a dark pattern.Dark patterns are deceptive designs in apps and websites that push people into making choices they didn't intend to make, like hidden fees or hard-to-cancel subscriptions.The CCPA found that messages displayed on the app, including "Adding a tip might help increase the chances of getting a ride faster" and "Tip now to boost the chances of getting a ride sooner", gave users the impression that offering a tip could improve their chances of getting a ride.However, Ola's own booking data for June 1-15, 2026, showed otherwise. Ride requests with an add-on had acceptance rates of 38% in Delhi, 40% in Bengaluru and 39% in Mumbai.The rates for bookings without an add-on were significantly higher at 62%, 68% and 68%, respectively.The CCPA said Ola's position was contradictory. While the company maintained that additional payments did not influence ride allocation, its app interface suggested that paying extra could help secure a ride sooner.The authority, headed by Chief Commissioner Nidhi Khare and Commissioner Anupam Mishra, also found that suggested additional payments had risen from Rs 10-40 in May 2025 to as much as Rs 140. Users were also allowed to make payments of up to Rs 499.It identified the practice as 'Confirm Shaming', a dark pattern that creates fear or guilt among consumers for refusing to make an additional payment.The CCPA also held that the feature violated the Motor Vehicles Aggregators Guidelines, 2025, which allow tipping only after a journey has been completed.It directed Ola to withdraw all pre-ride payment prompts, regardless of whether they are described as tips, add-ons or additional fares.The authority has also initiated suo motu proceedings against other cab aggregators. It has imposed a Rs 10 lakh penalty on Rapido, while investigations into Uber and Namma Yatri are ongoing.Money habits form by age 7. Is your child learning the right ones? articles.title: Vanguard warning: Retirees are making costly mistakes with their 401(k)s
articles.summary: Many retirees have their 401(k) account investments "misaligned" for their life stage, according to new research from Vanguard.
articles.body:
Throughout your working years, you're constantly pushed to save in an employer's 401(k) plan. And that's a good thing.

Your employer may have automatically enrolled you in the plan when you were a new hire and annually bumped up how much you set aside from your paycheck.

When you finally retire, it can be difficult to pivot from that save, save, save mindset. Roughly 4 in 10 retirees are invested in portfolios that skew either very aggressive or very conservative for their stage of life.

A quarter had more than 80% of their balance in equities, while 16% held less than 30%, a range "potentially misaligned for most retirees," according to new research from Vanguard.

Retirees with balances of at least $1 million were three times more likely than those with lower amounts to have an aggressive allocation — keeping more than 80% of their balance in equities.

"This shows how haphazard individual investors can be with their retirement account allocations, [when] left to their own devices," Tyson Sprick, a financial planner in Overland Park, Kan., told Yahoo Finance. "The numbers make it clear that a large number of retirement plan participants are in a suboptimal situation. Having a plan for decumulation i s critical, and it should take shape years before actually retiring."

That process of shifting your retirement funds into a steady income stream to cover your living expenses after you stop working is a stumbling block for most retirees.

Keeping too much money in stocks can hurt if the market drops early in retirement, but too little can make it harder to keep up with inflation over 25 or 30 years.

"Many of today's retirees may have started saving in their retirement plan prior to target-date funds being offered or serving as the investment default," said Jeff Clark, head of defined contribution research at Vanguard.

"They've been self-directing their investment allocations throughout their career and may need to revisit whether their current allocation accurately reflects and supports their goals, income needs, and risk tolerance."

Target-date funds are a "set it and forget it" vehicle to invest savings based on a retirement year you pick — say, when you turn 67, the full retirement age for most of us. The fund shifts an account's investments from stocks to more fixed income and less volatile choices, such as cash and bonds, as you age.

Most of these retirees also do not touch their accounts once they exit the workplace. Roughly 8 in 10 retirees had taken no distributions from their accounts. Only 7% received regular installment payments.

articles.title: Wholesale inflation rose in October to highest annual rate in nearly four years
articles.summary: High energy prices continue to ripple through US supply chains, raising the costs for businesses and setting the stage for further increases in the coming months for American consumers.
articles.body: High energy prices continue to ripple through US supply chains, raising the costs for businesses and setting the stage for further increases in the coming months for American consumers. Wholesale inflation accelerated last month to its highest rate in nearly four years, Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed Friday. The Producer Price Index, a measurement of average price changes received by producers and manufacturers, rose 0.3% from the month before and 6.5% for the 12 months ended in October, the highest annual rate since November 2022. Excluding gas and food prices, core PPI rose 0.3% on a monthly basis and 5% annually, matching a rate last seen in January 2023. The Iran war and the resulting energy supply shock have sent gas and diesel prices markedly higher in recent months. Fuel prices didn’t rise as quickly last month as they did in September (when PPI rose at a breakneck rate of 1.4% to reach 6.3%); however, the past months’ surge, coupled with other more persistent price pressures, kept wholesale inflation quite elevated. Notably, food prices climbed rapidly higher for the second consecutive month, rising 1.3% in October – the fastest monthly hike since July 2022 – after increasing 1.1% in September. Within food, the largest price spikes were seen for produce products, which are primarily transported via truck. Freight transportation costs for the trucking industry are up nearly 25% from last year, BLS data shows. Friday’s report showed that prices for wholesale fresh and dry vegetables jumped 26.7% in October, following a 30.7% leap in September. The high diesel costs continue to flow to other categories, lifting costs for transportation, warehousing and key inputs like chemicals. More price hikes could come in 2027 While PPI doesn’t translate directly to the Consumer Price Index, its trajectory and category-specific price hikes can serve as a potential bellwether for what consumers could experience in near future. “We’ve seen a lot of pass-through already in places like airfares, where consumer prices have risen a lot,” Matt Bush, US economist at Guggenheim Investments, told CNN in an interview. However, the higher transportation and input costs businesses are seeing now might not hit consumers for another six to eight months, he said. “And it’s complicated by the fact that we also have some lingering tariff effects on a lot of these consumer goods prices,” he said. As a result, consumers could be in store for further sticker shock early next year. “That’s when the majority of businesses do their annual price resets,” he said. “In the case of the energy shock, there was an expectation that it could be short-lived; but given it’s gone on for several months now, I think as we head into the new year that you will see a lot of businesses deciding they need to pass on at least some of these costs.” At the same time, the massive investment in artificial intelligence technology and equipment are contributing another layer of inflationary pressures both for businesses and consumers. Electronic components and accessories, which rose at a six-month high pace of 4.2%, are up 31.7% from the year before, the highest annual rate on record, according to BLS data that goes back to December 1966. “Those don’t pass through as directly into consumer prices; but indirectly, we are seeing it show up in computer prices, TV prices, software prices,” Bush said. Friday’s PPI data, coupled with the hotter-than-expected October CPI released earlier this week, are expected to result in a rate hike from the Federal Reserve when policymakers meet in early December. Markets are expecting a quarter-point hike; however, Fed Governor Christopher Waller indicated earlier this week that a half-point hike could be necessary. The rate hikes might not end with December, said Ben Ayers, Nationwide senior economist. “Lingering impacts from the spike in fuel prices could linger into 2027, warranting further tightening by the Fed to limit second and third order inflation impacts,” he wrote in a note Friday.
