articles.title: 27.1% to 2.6%: India records one of world’s fastest poverty declines. It’s significant, but there’s a catch
articles.summary: India, among the world’s biggest economies, has also made significant strides in reducing poverty, especially extreme poverty in recent years.
articles.body: India, among the world’s biggest economies, has also made significant strides in reducing poverty, especially extreme poverty in recent years. According to the latest World Bank report, India has managed to achieve one of the fastest poverty declines in the world - in both monetary and non-monetary dimensions.Garibi hathao has been a slogan for decades, and now with extreme poverty falling from 27.1% to 2.6% between 2011 and 2023, the question is how far India has come in its fight against poverty, and how much further it still needs to go.India’s remarkable poverty decline in numbersHow is poverty defined? Poverty in India, as well as in assessments by multilateral institutions, is measured with reference to specified poverty lines or thresholds.The World Bank currently defines the international extreme poverty line at $3.00 per person per day in 2021 purchasing power parity (PPP) terms. According to the World Poverty Clock, extreme poverty may be considered eliminated when the poverty headcount ratio falls below 3%.With the World Bank estimating India’s extreme poverty rate at about 2% in 2024, India can, on this measure, be considered to have crossed that threshold.Between 2011 and 2023, the proportion of Indians living below the Lower Middle-Income Country poverty threshold of $4.20 a day (2021 PPP) dropped from 57.7% to 16.1%. This decline lifted an estimated 496 million people out of poverty. Over the same period, extreme poverty, measured against the $3-a-day threshold, fell from 27.1% to 2.6%.“Poverty is projected to continue declining, albeit more gradually, with the poverty rate at the $4.20/day line expected to fall from 14.2 per cent in 2026 to 12.1 per cent by 2028,” World Bank has said in its report.Not just that, India has also recorded big improvements in non-monetary indicators of poverty. According to the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative’s (OPHI) Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), the poverty rate fell from 53.8% in 2005-06 to 16.4% in 2019-21. The World Bank’s MPI measure put the rate at 15.5% in 2022-23.“As poverty declined, it became increasingly concentrated among households with lower education, fewer assets, limited access to stable employment, and higher dependency ratios. Wage disparities, however, remain pronounced, as median earnings among the top 10 per cent of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10 per cent in 2023,” the report says.How did India reduce poverty significantly?The World Bank says progress was mainly driven by strong consumption growth, rising employment, especially among women, and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies. India's poverty reduction story is one of both convergence and concentration.“Households in both rural and urban areas experienced substantial welfare gains, with faster progress in rural India significantly narrowing the rural-urban gap. Yet many of the households that remain poor continue to live in rural areas, where productivity is lower and access to higher-quality non-farm employment opportunities remain more limited,” the report says.Experts say the decline in poverty reflects a combination of income and employment growth, together with an extensive social protection system, including subsidised food provision and rural employment support.DK Srivastava, Chief Policy Advisor, EY India says rural employment guarantee programme, earlier known as MGNREGA and presently referred to as VB-G-RAM-G, has also played an important role.“India’s domestic approach to measuring poverty has traditionally used consumption thresholds consistent with minimum nutritional requirements and expenditure on specified non-food items. In 2011-12, the Rangarajan Committee re-estimated these poverty thresholds, with separate poverty lines for rural and urban areas and variations across states. These thresholds were substantially higher than the international extreme poverty line,” he explains.Recent studies have updated the Rangarajan Committee-based poverty lines to 2022-23.For example, a recent RBI study provides poverty estimates for 19 states using updated rural and urban poverty thresholds.“On a population-weighted basis across these states, the poverty headcount ratio declined from 31.1% to 6.7% in rural areas and from 26.9% to 6.8% in urban areas,” he tells TOI, adding that several factors have contributed to this substantial decline.Apart from broader income and employment growth, important policy interventions include the rural employment guarantee programme and the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PMGKAY).While Direct Benefit Transfer allows the government to transfer welfare benefits, subsidies and other payments directly to beneficiaries’ bank accounts, the Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (PM-GKAY) aims to provide free foodgrains to eligible households.State governments have also implemented income-transfer and subsidy programmes targeted at lower-income households.“The free food scheme has released resources for spending on other goods and services. Further, we have created new low paying but still income generating jobs in new sectors which have been booming like ecommerce, logistics and construction. This has added to income and spending power,” explains Madan Sabnavis, Chief economist, Bank of Baroda.“Governments have paid attention to welfare which is needed at a time when the private system is unable to create jobs for all,” he adds.Yet another major factor has been the accelerated capital expenditure by the government over the years.“This has been a significant contributor to impacting poverty. It has connected farms to markets and has led to better realisations for the farmers,” says Ranen Banerjee, Partner and Leader, Economic Advisory, PwC India.Besides, it has allowed mobility of labour to urban areas for casual labour besides directly generating construction jobs.Then, there are the multiplier effects of sectoral growth.“The growth of the service sector and services exports have also created several organised sector jobs that has led to several multiples of unorganised sector jobs and this has also supported poverty alleviation,” Ranen Banerjee tells TOI.Has this translated into a better standard of living?Experts say there is little doubt that the standard of living has gone up.“When free food is given, people have money to spend on other goods which would have otherwise gone for food. Similarly cash transfers and free travel have helped women to go out and work and led to better utilization of income. Therefore, there has been genuine improvement,” Madan Sabnavis tells TOI.Changes in the composition of household consumption provide one indication that the decline in poverty has been accompanied by broader improvements in living standards.DK Srivastava explains that one way to assess this is through the changing composition of private final consumption expenditure (PFCE).Food, beverages and tobacco accounted for nearly 60% of total PFCE in the early 1960s; by the 2020s, their share had fallen to less than half.At the same time, the share of non-food consumption has increased, including spending on transport, education, health, and miscellaneous goods and services.“This shift from basic necessities towards a more diversified consumption basket is generally consistent with rising household incomes and improved living standards,” he says.In fact, the structural shift has been particularly noticeable over the past two-and-a-half decades, from around 2000-01 onwards. While changes in consumption composition alone do not capture every dimension of household welfare, they provide supporting evidence that improvements in living standards have accompanied the measured decline in poverty.What’s the road ahead?While the decline in poverty is an important achievement, as they famously say: one can't afford to rest on our laurels.India, too, has a long road ahead.The World Bank report also notes that poverty has also become increasingly concentrated geographically.“While living standards improved across most states, households in a contiguous belt stretching from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal account for about 57 per cent of India’s poor population. As a result, further reductions in national poverty will increasingly depend on enabling productive employment in these states.” it says.Poverty decline and growth in jobs are two different things. And the next phase of India’s poverty alleviation programme needs to be associated with economic growth that enables higher jobs and income.Between 2017 and 2023, the number of employed people rose by approximately 134 million, which is nearly twice the increase in the working-age population.A substantial part of this expansion has come from rural women entering paid employment, increasing the number of income earners within households, the World Bank reports says.Labour market conditions have remained broadly resilient, with labour force participation and employment rates staying stable between the first quarters of FY2026 and FY2027.However, the World Bank report notes that youth unemployment rose from 14.6 to 15.9 per cent between the two quarters, particularly among rural young women.“Moreover, real earnings remained broadly unchanged with employment growth concentrated in relatively low-productivity activities,” it adds.The catch is that government-backed programmes have been a big contributor to the decline in poverty. So the next question is, can governments keep doing what they are forever?“If the food scheme is stopped, the Rs 2 lakh crore of subsidy will be withdrawn which means that people will slip down the income ladder. This is the major challenge of free cash/food. While they help a lot and can be accommodated in budgets, any cutback will risk making these people slip downwards. This is a challenge for us as we may not be having a skilled labour force in line with requirements of industry,” cautions Sabnavis.Ranen Banerjee pitches for focus on spending on public health, skilling and education to support the households to come out of the poverty trap and get into gainful employment.“The health insurance scheme is a very effective measure to prevent poorer households from falling back into the poverty trap owing to healthcare expenses derailing their upward mobility,” he tells TOI.What’s important to understand is that India’s transition to upper-middle-income status will require sustained economic growth combined with higher labour-force participation, productivity improvements, technological absorption and continued investment in human capital.The World Bank’s lower threshold for the upper-middle-income category is $4,636 per capita at market exchange rates for 2026-27.India’s per capita GDP in 2026-27 is estimated at around $2,759 at market exchange rates and $12,998 in 2021 purchasing power parity terms.Srivastava says that continuation of policies directed towards achieving developed-country status could enable India to cross the upper-middle-income threshold by the mid-2030s.Three areas would be particularly important:First, India would need to sustain real GDP growth of around 6-7% over an extended period.Second, greater participation of women in productive employment could significantly expand the effective labour force and support household incomes and economic growth.Third, India will need to manage the potential employment disruptions associated with rapid technological change, including artificial intelligence.“This will require greater investment in research and development, faster adoption of technologies already available globally, and substantial investment in skilling and re-skilling the workforce. Together, these measures can help raise productivity and incomes while ensuring that technological progress translates into broad-based employment and income gains,” the EY expert tells TOI.Robert Frost famously wrote, ‘miles to go before I sleep.’ To borrow from the poet, India still has miles to go before it is out of the woods on the poverty front.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Bessent: Treasury pushed to blacklist Megaspeed, but ‘Commerce has the pen’
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is pointing the finger at Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the Trump administration’s failure to place Nvidia customer Megaspeed on a U.S. trade blacklist for national security concerns. When pressed Friday over who was behind the decision, Bessent told CNBC, “Treasury, War, USTR [U.S. Trade Representative] and State … were in…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is pointing the finger at Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the Trump administration’s failure to place Nvidia customer Megaspeed on a U.S. trade blacklist for national security concerns .

When pressed Friday over who was behind the decision, Bessent told CNBC, “Treasury, War, USTR [U.S. Trade Representative] and State … were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months.”

“But Commerce has the pen. Commerce BIS has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent added, referring to the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security.

The remarks follow a report earlier this week detailing potential tensions between the two Cabinet members. Axios reported that Bessent approached Lutnick about the failure to place the Singaporean cloud computing and data center firm Megaspeed on the entity list earlier this month.

Lutnick told Bessent he would “look into it,” Axios reported. Citing anonymous sources, Axios further reported Lutnick spent the last year “undoing” efforts within the Trump administration to scrutinize Megaspeed, as he was concerned it would impact the U.S.’s trade war with China.

Megaspeed was thrown into the spotlight this month after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang seemingly admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a onetime Megaspeed executive who U.S. officials concluded was a Chinese spy.

The New York Times later reported the former CEO had a second affair with a direct report, and Jensen Huang stepped down from his role Thursday morning.

Lawmakers are calling on Huang and Lutnick to testify before Congress. The Commerce secretary has “ proactively agreed to appear voluntarily” before the Senate Banking Committee, spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said in a statement to The Hill on Friday.

Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) sent letters to both Lutnick and Huang on Thursday, asking them to appear before the committee early next month.

“Given the Department of Commerce’s central role in issuing and enforcing export control regulations, your testimony before the Committee will be essential to our oversight of these efforts,” Scott wrote.

articles.title: Cartier-owner Richemont stock slips as luxury jewelry sales slow
articles.summary: Luxury brands are struggling. Richemont's jewelry business is feeling a bit of the pinch this year.
articles.body:
Richemont stock opened more than 4% lower on Friday morning as the Swiss luxury group reported slower growth in its jewelry business.

The owner of Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels posted first-half net profit of 2.5 billion euros (approximately $2.76 billion), up from 1.8 billion euros ($2 billion) a year earlier and above analyst forecasts of 2.26 billion euros ($2.5 billion).

But eyes were on jewelry, the group's growth engine, where sales rose 14%, short of the 16% analysts had expected, according to an RBC poll.

Many luxury brands have struggled amid foreign conflicts, rising gold prices, and cost-sensitive consumers. The luxury sector has fallen some 30% in 2026, per Barron's.

However, on Friday, the Swiss company's leadership pointed to the strength of the results. "Richemont delivered strong results in a volatile geopolitical and macroeconomic environment," Richemont chairman Johann Rupert said.

The shortfall in jewelry sales largely came from the Middle East, especially the United Arab Emirates market. Second quarter sales in the region fell 7% from 22% growth a year earlier, as geopolitical tensions escalated over the summer.

"Clearly, destinations that were relying on touristic purchases have been hurt the most," CEO Nicolas Bos said on Friday's call, pointing to Dubai's malls. Every other region grew by double digits.

Costs are also a pressure point. Gold prices ( GC=F ) pushed up production costs, though price increases and a better sales mix largely offset them. Meanwhile, the company's watch division, soft in recent years, grew 12%.

Analysts appeared more forgiving than the market. Quilter Cheviot analyst Mamta Valechha noted that peers have averaged just 1% to 2% organic growth this quarter, making 14% "a relatively strong outperformance." Bernstein called the results "excellent" and said Richemont remains "head and shoulders above" its major rivals.

articles.title: US Treasury warns against rate hikes during US-Iran war energy ‘shock’
articles.summary: Despite Treasury’s Scott Bessent’s remarks, financial tracker CME Fed Watch forecasts rate hike in December likely.
articles.body:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called on the Federal Reserve not to hike interest rates because of an “energy supply shock” tied to the US-led conflict with Iran.

“I think the Fed should understand that this is an energy supply shock,” while the underlying US economy is very strong, Bessent said in an interview on CNBC on Friday.

“So I think that to hike too much into an energy supply shock when it’s coming down, these are very noisy numbers,” he said. “The Fed’s supposed to look into the future, not look in the rearview mirror.”

The central bank opted to maintain interest rates during its last policy meeting, leaving them at 3.75 to 4 percent. CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, forecasts an 89.4 percent chance that rates will be raised to 4.00–4.25 percent at the next meeting, scheduled for December 9.

Despite pressure from the White House to cut interest rates, the Federal Reserve has held them steady amid inflationary pressures stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran . Since the conflict began, the Fed has maintained rates five times and raised them once.

Much of that pressure has come from rising energy prices. By September, energy prices had climbed 20.4 percent year over year. Although October’s energy price data has since been released, the Labour Department was unable to collect data in October 2025 because of last year’s government shutdown. As a result, it cannot provide a year-over-year comparison for October 2026.

Bessent’s remarks come amid a stronger-than-expected US jobs report, which bolsters the case for rate hikes. The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Labour Department’s release last Friday.

“I’m not going to tell the Fed what to do. I am going to say they should have an open mind,” Bessent said.

The Fed made three rate cuts over the same period last year, he noted.

“And now to reverse just based on an energy supply shock, a reversal in a dramatic way isn’t something that I would do if I were on the Fed. But I’m not on the Fed.”

Bessent’s remarks come as some top Fed officials are pushing for the opposite. On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he planned to support a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting unless the core consumer price index — one of the central bank’s key measures for assessing the rate of inflation — came in at 0.3 percent or more.

“In that case, I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting,” he said at a conference in London hosted by King’s Business School and the Money Macro and Finance Society.

The CPI report subsequently came out, showing a 0.4 percent monthly increase.

Consumers are feeling the rising costs at the petrol pump, as prices are declining but remain high. The average price for a gallon of petrol is $3.87 ($1.02 per litre), down from $4.34 ($1.14 per litre)this time a month ago, but still well above the $2.98 ($0.79 per litre) price recorded on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.

articles.title: The fight over Canadian steelworker jobs
articles.summary: Stelco’s US owner blames Trump’s tariffs for layoffs, but its support for those same tariffs has raised questions.
articles.body:
Hamilton, Ontario, Canada – Chelsey Masteij had heard layoffs might be coming at Stelco, so she decided to use up some of her vacation days. She was making the most of the time off with her new dog when she got a call telling her not to come back to work.

The 34-year-old had spent years trying to break into the male-dominated steel industry before finally landing a job at the company’s Hamilton plant about three years ago.

She started as a general labourer in the cold-rolling department, later training to operate cranes and taking on shifts in the coke ovens.

The work was gruelling and physically demanding, but Masteij grew to love the routine and the close-knit community of coworkers she came to consider family. When she shared photos of herself with Al Jazeera, all in protective gear at the plant, she joked that she hardly had any pictures outside of work.

Masteij thought she might stay at Stelco until retirement. Instead, she was laid off on October 9.

The news hit hard, and she spent much of the next two weeks sleeping.

“I was in a complete mess,” she told Al Jazeera, her voice cracking as she recalled the experience. “I was kind of depressed.”

Now, instead of working 12-hour shifts, Masteij spends much of her time at home, cutting back on expenses while she collects employment insurance.

Masteij is among hundreds of Canadian steelworkers facing layoffs after Stelco’s American owner, Cleveland-Cliffs, announced in late September that it would temporarily shut down parts of its operations in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ontario.

Stelco blames the move on United States President Donald Trump’s tariffs, which it says have made it harder to sell Canadian steel to US customers, and on competition from cheaper foreign steel entering Canada.

But government officials and plant workers, including Masteij, are not convinced that is the whole story.

“Right now, there are a lot of lies going on with what’s happened,” Masteij said.

While US tariffs have hurt the Canadian steel industry, the union representing Stelco workers questions whether Cleveland-Cliffs is using difficult market conditions to serve its own business interests, with Canadian workers paying the price.

“Everyone knows we’re being used as pawns, that these layoffs weren’t necessary,” said Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, speaking to Al Jazeera at his Hamilton office.

In June 2025, Trump doubled tariffs on steel and aluminium imports, including from Canada, to 50 percent, making them more expensive for US buyers.

According to Stelco, Canada’s exports of cold-rolled and coated steel to the US – used to make everything from cars to building materials – fell by 58 percent in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the quarterly average before the trade war.

But demand has also fallen in Canada, where the auto industry, a major buyer of the cold-rolled steel produced at the Hamilton plant, has also been hit hard by Trump’s tariffs, said Colin Mang, an assistant professor of economics at McMaster University in Hamilton.

“When they say that there is less demand for the product coming out of the Hamilton mill, that is correct,” Mang told Al Jazeera.

But it is not just Trump’s tariffs that Cleveland-Cliffs blames for Stelco’s problems.

During a July earnings call, CEO Lourenco Goncalves warned that the company might scale back production in Canada unless Ottawa did more to protect its steel industry from imports.

“And that will have consequences for employment in Canada, but will have a positive financial impact on Stelco and on Cleveland-Cliffs,” he said.

That was the first time Wells had heard jobs might be at risk. The union later offered to help Cleveland-Cliffs lobby Ottawa for stronger protections against foreign steel imports, believing Canadian workers might have more sway with the government.

“They never took us up on our offer,” Wells said.

Instead, the next call brought news of the layoffs.

As of Saturday, 175 workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant had received layoff notices, with the announced cuts expected to affect up to 500 workers there and in Nanticoke.

Late last month, about 30 attended an information session the union organised in Hamilton, where they could learn about employment insurance and retraining opportunities.

Many were frustrated by the lack of clarity about how long the shutdown would last.

Some asked how their benefits would compare to their wages, while others wondered whether they would qualify for the full amount.

For workers who had spent decades at Stelco, another daunting prospect loomed: having to look for work for the first time in the digital era, competing for jobs with younger applicants as they neared retirement.

Some are already considering heading out west to find work.

“It’s hard for them to make those decisions,” Wells said, describing what he had been hearing from members. “Do I leave my family, go out west, make some money? Because they don’t know how long this is going to be.”

Masteij worries about what that could mean for Hamilton, a city where generations of families have worked in steelmaking, an industry that has shaped its identity for more than a century.

“I’m a steel city girl, and I can’t imagine the city without steel manufacturing,” she said. “We are losing tradesmen.”

But as workers grapple with what the layoffs mean for their families and their city, the union has been asking another question: whether these layoffs needed to happen at all – and it is not alone.

The US company has come under fire from the Canadian government, which is threatening legal action, accusing it of breaking promises it made when it bought Stelco in 2024.

Those included keeping at least the same number of unionised jobs and most non-unionised jobs in Canada, and pushing for trade policies that would benefit the steel industries in both Canada and the US.

Cleveland-Cliffs denies violating the agreement, saying it expects to meet its employment commitments for the year. It also maintains the layoffs are needed to “ensure the survival of Stelco” amid US tariffs, weaker demand and competition from cheaper foreign steel.

But the union and the government point to Stelco’s recent financial performance. Earlier this month, Goncalves reported the company’s strongest quarter since the acquisition.

“Mr Goncalves is not a victim,” Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly told Canada’s public broadcaster CBC, pointing to the company’s earnings. “He’s never made so much money.”

Experts have also challenged Goncalves’s claim that Canadian steelmakers are struggling because of “an avalanche of imports”.

Mang points out that nearly 80 percent of Canada’s cold-rolled steel imports come from the US, as does about half of the galvanised and painted steel coming into the country.

“What he’s trying to sell people on is the idea that there’s all this European or Asian steel coming into Canada,” he said. “This stuff is coming from his own country.”

The union and the government have also asked why, as Goncalves pushes for stronger protections in Canada against foreign steel, he has also been a vocal supporter of Trump’s tariffs on Canadian steel.

In testimony to US lawmakers in January, Goncalves argued that no country, including Canada, should be exempted from the steel tariffs. In an interview with Politico last year, he said he was “very happy” with the 50 percent tariffs on steel imports, adding, “I have my fingerprints on that 50 percent.”

For Wells, the irony is that Goncalves helped create the same conditions Cleveland-Cliffs now blames for the layoffs. He believes the company is using Canadian workers to pressure Ottawa to impose more restrictions on foreign steel, while also helping Trump argue that his tariffs are working.

Mang explained why Goncalves’ seemingly contradictory position might make sense for Cleveland-Cliffs.

“He wants trade barriers in both countries to seal off their domestic markets from each other and also from the rest of the world,” Mang said, “so that his companies in each country can benefit in their own domestic markets.”

Cleveland-Cliffs has been under growing pressure from Ottawa, which gave the company 15 days from October 22 to honour its commitments to Canadian workers or face legal action.

Amid that pressure, comments Goncalves made to CBC late last month appeared to support the union’s suspicions that the layoffs have less to do with tough market conditions and more to do with Cleveland-Cliffs’ broader business interests.

Asked why he supported tariffs on Canadian steel despite promises to protect workers and advocate for the Canadian steel industry when Cleveland-Cliffs bought Stelco, he said: “I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company.”

The admission caught the attention of Joly, who said the comments could strengthen the government’s case against Cleveland-Cliffs if Goncalves meant that he had bought Stelco to keep its Canadian operations idle. She added that Ottawa could force the company to sell its Canadian assets.

On November 6, as Ottawa’s 15-day deadline expired, Joly asked Canada’s Competition Bureau to investigate the 2024 acquisition and whether the company’s conduct violated Canadian competition law.

“If negotiations and acquisition were conducted in bad faith, Canadians deserve to know. The company needs to face the consequences,” she said in a statement.

Cleveland-Cliffs maintains that it has complied with its obligations under the Investment Canada Act.

Goncalves has rejected the prospect of a forced sale but suggested he might sell Stelco himself in a year.

“I will sell the company after we operate the company for a while, and now that I know that I’m persona non grata in Canada, I will do that,” he told CBC.

In a statement to The Canadian Press news agency late last month, he said he hoped to bring laid-off workers back before Christmas.

“It will depend on Canadian customers buying Canadian steel, made by Stelco,” he said.

Al Jazeera contacted Cleveland-Cliffs for comment on the union’s allegations and Goncalves’s remarks.

For Masteij, even as she waits to hear whether she will be recalled, she is preparing for the possibility that her time at Stelco is done. Her low seniority means she would be one of the last to be called back.

Masteij plans to use the time she is eligible for employment insurance to take a heavy equipment training programme, hoping it will open the door to other opportunities and give her something to focus on. The training could also help her if she returns to Stelco, which is still what she is hoping for.

For Wells, what is especially frustrating is how the company is treating workers, given the years of hard work and sacrifices many have made in their jobs.

“It’s not glamorous. You work shifts, nights, days, in the hot and the cold,” he said. “Our members miss Christmas meals with their families or their kids’ hockey games because they’re expected to work.”

“And that’s why this is particularly tough because that loyalty isn’t being repaid,” Wells added. “It’s actually being exploited, if anything.”

He worries about what a drawn-out legal battle could mean for those workers.

“Our members don’t have a lot of time,” he said. “We’re hoping things get settled as soon as possible.”

articles.title: Social Security cuts: 28 states could lose $500 or more per month
articles.summary: New reports reveal which states face the biggest Social Security benefit cuts in 2032 and what Congress could do to fix the shortfall.
articles.body:

If you rely on Social Security to pay your bills, a looming shortfall could cost you more than $6,000 a year, depending on where you live.

An analysis from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) shows which states could suffer the biggest cuts. Meanwhile, new AARP research suggests the program's financial insolvency could have been postponed by decades if one simple measure was taken years ago.

With Social Security's main trust fund expected to run out of reserves in 2032, lawmakers face mounting pressure to find a solution. But proposals have failed to gain traction in Congress.

Social Security's retirement and survivors trust fund is projected to exhaust its reserves in late 2032, according to the 2026 Social Security trustees report .

That doesn't mean Social Security will go bankrupt or stop paying benefits. Instead, incoming revenue from payroll taxes and other sources could only cover about 78% of scheduled retirement and survivor benefits.

Without congressional action, that translates to a potential 22% benefit reduction.

A CRFB analysis , which used a slightly higher 24% reduction based on an earlier projection, found that the average monthly benefit could get cut by more than $500 in 28 states and Washington, D.C.

Nationwide, the average cut would be $500 a month, with losses ranging from $459 in Mississippi to $556 in Connecticut. In reality, the report finds "if Social Security becomes insolvent – no state would be spared."

The report also found that benefit reductions would impact roughly 1 in 5 Americans and result in $345 billion in lost payments annually, equivalent to 1.1% of the nation's gross domestic product (GDP).

Connecticut tops CRFB's rankings at $556 a month, followed by New Jersey and New Hampshire.

Here are the 10 states facing the largest average reductions under the CRFB's hypothetical 24% cut.

Why some states face larger benefit cuts

Social Security retirement benefits are partly based on a worker's lifetime earnings, so if you earned more, you tend to receive more in retirement.

That means people who get bigger Social Security checks would lose more money each month on a dollar-for-dollar basis, even if everyone's benefits were cut by the same percentage.

For example, someone collecting $2,300 a month would lose $552 under a 24% cut. Someone receiving $1,900 would see a smaller $456 reduction.

But smaller dollar losses still hurt, especially in lower-income states where retirees may have less savings to cushion the blow. Mississippi has the lowest estimated monthly cut, $459, yet total benefit losses would equal 1.8% of its economy, according to the CRFB.

The estimates come with some important caveats, though.

The CRFB used Social Security beneficiary data and state economic figures from 2024 to model a hypothetical 24% benefit cut. Actual losses in 2032 would depend on changes in beneficiary demographics, benefit amounts, and economic conditions.

The latest trustees report also projects a slightly smaller funding shortfall of 22%.

The most populous states could lose the most money overall.

Under the CRFB's scenario, annual benefit losses could be greatest in these states.

Source: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB)

When measured as a percentage of a state's GDP, however, a different group of states faces the biggest impact.

Maine also has the largest share of residents affected, at 22.9%, versus 17.7% nationally.

Social Security won't stop collecting taxes or paying benefits in 2032. But its reserves are drying up.

The program is primarily funded through payroll taxes paid by workers and employers. When revenue exceeds benefit payments and other costs, the surplus is credited to Social Security's trust funds, which hold special-issue U.S. Treasury securities.

When expenses exceed income, Social Security can redeem those securities to cover the difference.

A slate of reforms in 1983 helped build a cushion that peaked in 2020. But program costs have exceeded total income since 2021, and the retirement and survivors trust fund could exhaust its reserves by late 2032.

Incoming revenue would then cover about 78% of scheduled retirement and survivor payments.

Social Security's separate disability trust fund remains solvent over the long term under current projections.

If the retirement and disability funds were combined, their reserves would last until 2034, at which point incoming revenue would cover about 83% of combined scheduled benefits.

AARP research highlights another cause of Social Security's financial woes: A shrinking share of the economy is subject to payroll taxes.

In 1984, taxable payroll accounted for about 41% of U.S. GDP. By 2025, that share was just 34%.

If taxable payroll had remained at its 1984 share of GDP, Social Security would have collected an additional $10.8 trillion between 1984 and 2034, measured in inflation-adjusted 2025 dollars, according to AARP estimates.

That money could have kept the combined retirement and disability funds solvent until 2059 — 25 years longer. It's a hypothetical scenario, not a guarantee.

AARP points to rising business and investment income, automation, and business structures that allow some owners to receive profits rather than wages. Much of that income escapes Social Security payroll taxes.

That's a major loss for a program that depends heavily on workers' earnings — 91% of Social Security's revenue came from payroll taxes in 2025.

One solution is to raise the payroll tax rate.

Yet, for over 35 years, the combined payroll tax rate hasn't budged. It's been 12.4% — split equally between employers and employees — since 1990, with an exception for a temporary payroll tax reduction in 2011 and 2012.

There's also a ceiling on earnings subject to Social Security taxes. That limit is $184,500 in 2026 and will rise to $192,300 in 2027.

The Social Security trustees have also estimated that immediately raising the combined payroll tax rate to 16.65% — 4.25% higher, split equally between employers and employees — at the beginning of 2026 would have kept the trust funds solvent for over 75 years.

But increasing payroll taxes is just one of several options on the table for lawmakers.

Congress has several ways to shore up Social Security's finances, including increasing taxes, changing benefit formulas, or raising the retirement age.

Each option comes with economic and political trade-offs.

Bipartisan reform is possible — it happened in 1983. Those reforms accelerated payroll tax increases, gradually increased the full retirement age from 65 to 67, and taxed some benefits.

Those changes were expected to keep the program solvent into the early 2060s. Now, trust funds are projected to exhaust their reserves nearly three decades sooner.

The looming funding shortfall is prompting new bipartisan discussions in Washington, but lawmakers remain divided over how to actually close the funding gap.

The PROMISE Act would establish a process for developing and considering legislation designed to provide at least 50 years of Social Security solvency.

But so far, Congress hasn't passed a comprehensive plan to resolve the program's financial crisis.

Various legislation has been proposed in recent years to fix Social Security, including:

Eliminate the payroll tax cap: Sens. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., have proposed taxing all wages but haven't introduced a bill. But the Tax Policy Center warns that insolvency would only be postponed.

Tax high incomes and expand benefits: The 2026 Social Security 2100 Act from Rep. John Larson, D-Conn., and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., would tax more earnings above $400,000 and certain investment income while increasing benefits and revising cost-of-living adjustments.

Use estate tax revenue: The Strengthen Social Security by Taxing Dynastic Wealth Act, introduced in March 2026 by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., would restore federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes to their 2009 levels. It would raise the top estate tax rate from 40% to 45% and direct the additional funds to Social Security.

Invest through a separate fund: For decades, Sens. Bill Cassidy, R-La., and Tim Kaine, D-Va., have proposed a roughly $1.5 trillion Treasury-financed fund invested in the stock market. Higher returns could help provide the trust funds with more revenue, but poor returns could leave taxpayers holding the bag. The proposal doesn't solve the 2032 deadline on its own.

You shouldn't assume a 22% cut is inevitable. Congress could act before the trust fund's projected depletion date, and any reforms could impact current and future beneficiaries differently than expected.

But the shortfall highlights the risks of relying on Social Security completely for your retirement income.

Here are a few things you can do to prepare:

Contribute more to retirement accounts. Boosting your savings in a tax-advantaged retirement account, such as a 401(k) or IRA, can help reduce your reliance on Social Security. If your employer offers a 401(k) match, try to contribute enough to capture the match.

Get an updated Social Security benefit estimate: Create or log in to your my Social Security account to see how much you could receive in retirement based on your earnings history and expected claiming age. This can help you understand what a 22% cut really means for your wallet.

Stress-test your retirement budget: Estimating how a 22% benefit reduction would actually impact your monthly expenses can help you identify any potential shortfalls ahead of time.

There's no across-the-board cut currently scheduled to take effect. The retirement and survivors trust fund could exhaust reserves in late 2032, but Congress could change the rules before then.

The trustees project a 22% shortfall by 2032. So if you received $2,000 a month in Social Security, you could receive about $1,560 instead, though actual reductions may differ.

Without legislative changes, current retirees and survivor beneficiaries would also face reductions. Congress could protect current beneficiaries in a future deal, but that isn't guaranteed.

articles.title: Nvidia's Chris Malachowsky cofounded the company and is seen as a potential successor to Huang
articles.summary: Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky is one of many individuals who could take over the company as CEO.
articles.body:
With Jensen Huang out as Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO following his affair scandals, CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO.

The company's board is now searching both internally and externally for a permanent replacement for Huang.

Rene Haas, the CEO of Arm Holdings, is a contender , and Ian Buck, Nvidia's head of hyperscale and high-performance computing, is considered an early frontrunner for the position thanks to his strong technical expertise.

Buck created the CUDA software that enables developers to use Nvidia's chips for general-purpose computing, helping turn the company into the AI juggernaut it is today.

Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky could also step in to serve as CEO.

An accomplished engineer with nearly 40 patents to his name, Malachowsky is an Nvidia fellow and senior technology executive, a biography on the company's site states.

Malachowsky has overseen efforts within Nvidia, including its operations and engineering. He's also led its research organization.

But whether Malachowsky, or anyone, for that matter, can fully replace Huang remains to be seen. The former CEO was Nvidia's biggest champion and the face of the AI era.

He hosted enormous keynote events, clad in his signature leather jackets, and traveled the world, drawing massive crowds as an AI ambassador.

He also had the kind of deep connections necessary to attract customers and make investments in a variety of AI-related businesses.

For now, Kress will serve as a steadying force within Nvidia as it seeks to find its footing following the past week's drama.

But the company's board will have to make a decision sooner or later, and whoever it chooses will determine the future of one of the world's most important companies. Sounds easy.

articles.title: Stock market today: Nasdaq leads Dow, S&P 500 lower as chip stock sell-off accelerates
articles.summary: A bumpy week didn't prevent the major averages from pacing for weekly gains.
articles.body: US stocks fell Friday as a sell-off in chip stocks picked up, Nvidia (NVDA) stock continued to decline, and an annual reading of wholesale inflation came in hot.The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) edged lower by 0.2%, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC) declined 0.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) fell 1.6%.Stocks sank amid a series of tremors, from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepping down to elevated oil prices and a sell-off in government bonds. Nvidia stock turned lower again as the fallout from Huang's affairs continued to unfold, raising the stakes for the company's third quarter earnings next Tuesday. Investors are debating whether the controversy surrounding the chip giant's former leader implicates the wider artificial intelligence boom that Nvidia has played a central role in building.Chipmaker sector stocks declined, with AMD (AMD) and Broadcom (AVGO) sinking. Oil prices were little changed, providing some relief after a spike in prices sparked Thursday's sell-off in bonds. As traders braced for an interest rate hike in December, the 10-year Treasury yield (^TNX) reached as high as 5.17% on Friday, its highest level since October.The setup has pressured bitcoin (BTC), with the world's largest cryptocurrency tumbling below $70,000 Friday for the first time in nearly three months. In economic news, wholesale inflation rose 0.3% month over month in October, according to the producer price index. The reading was less than the 0.4% economists expected, but the annual rate of 6.5% highlighted persistent inflation pressures, which likely keeps the Federal Reserve on track to hike interest rates next month.
